ChatGPT said:

Ah, human languages. In that case, I'd probably pick Tamil—with a qualification that I don't literally have personal preferences.

Tamil is unusually interesting because it combines several things:

  • Very deep literary history — written literary traditions going back well over two millennia.

  • Continuity — it isn't simply an ancient language preserved in books; it remains a major living language.

  • Diglossia — the difference between formal/literary Tamil and everyday spoken varieties is unusually pronounced.

  • Strong grammatical tradition — Tolkāppiyam represents an extraordinarily early attempt to systematise Tamil grammar and poetics.

  • Large modern ecosystem — cinema, literature, journalism, computing, music and online communities all operate in Tamil.

  • And linguistically, it's particularly interesting because it belongs to the Dravidian family, giving us a window into a completely different branch of language evolution from Indo-European.

So if I had to choose one to study purely for intellectual interest: Tamil.

And yes, Elixir is a very defensible programming-language choice. Its combination of Erlang/BEAM concurrency, functional programming and OTP is quite unusual. The main reason it hasn't become mainstream isn't that it is technically poor; it's mostly the usual vicious cycle:

small ecosystem → fewer jobs → fewer developers → fewer libraries/companies → small ecosystem.

Its strengths become particularly compelling when the problem involves massive concurrency, fault tolerance, distributed systems or real-time services.


You said:

Give a table with some of the species that went extinct recently due to human, and what was the cause, what humans were responsible - if a corporate, or a country or region, etc, or a few individuals.

ChatGPT said:

Yes. If the question is "which species did humans drive extinct, and can we identify who actually did it?", the answer is surprisingly interesting because responsibility ranges from a handful of hunters to industrial markets and governments.

I've deliberately included cases where the human causal chain is reasonably well established, rather than blaming humans for every recent extinction.

SpeciesExtinctMain human-caused mechanismWho was responsible?How direct was it?
Steller's sea cow (Hydrodamalis gigas)1768Intensive hunting for meat by fur-trading expeditionsRussian fur traders / hunting crews operating in the Commander IslandsVery direct — a small number of hunting groups apparently exterminated the final population in ~27 years. Natural History Museum+1
Dodo (Raphus cucullatus)c. 1660s–1680sIntroduced rats, pigs, cats, dogs; habitat disturbance; some huntingDutch/European colonisation of Mauritius, particularly ships and settlers introducing animalsDirect, but mostly indirect ecological effects rather than simply hunting the birds. Natural History Museum+1
Great auk (Pinguinus impennis)1844/1852Mass hunting for meat, feathers, oil and eggs; later collectingEuropean/North Atlantic commercial hunters, followed by museums and private collectorsExtremely direct. The final breeding pair were killed by hunters in Iceland in 1844. Natural History Museum+1
Passenger pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius)1914Industrial-scale commercial hunting + deforestationUS commercial hunters, market hunters, farmers and expanding settlementVery direct, but distributed across a huge industry and population rather than one company. Smithsonian Magazine
Thylacine / Tasmanian tiger (Thylacinus cynocephalus)1936Persecution, bounty hunting, habitat change and competition/conflict with livestockTasmanian colonial government + settlers/farmers; the Van Diemen's Land Company introduced a bounty in 1830Very direct institutional responsibility. Tasmania Parks
Baiji / Yangtze river dolphin (Lipotes vexillifer)c. 2002By-catch, fishing gear, shipping, habitat degradation and industrialisation of the YangtzeDiffuse Chinese economic activity: fishing communities, industry, shipping and government development policy; not one perpetratorSystemic. China did enact protection measures, but enforcement and conservation efforts failed. iucn-csg.org

IUCN

Pyrenean ibex (Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica)2000Hunting, competition with livestock and diseaseHunters + agricultural/pastoral land use, primarily across Spain/FranceDiffuse, rather than attributable to a particular corporation or government.

The Steller's sea cow is probably the most astonishing example

It is almost a laboratory demonstration of how quickly humans can destroy a species.

The species had already been reduced to a tiny remnant population before Europeans encountered it. Then Russian maritime fur traders began using the Commander Islands as bases.

The remaining animals were enormous, slow, conspicuous and apparently didn't fear humans.

Researchers modelling the historical hunting records estimated that they were being harvested at more than seven times a sustainable rate. The final population disappeared by 1768. PubMed Central (PMC)+1

No corporation needed to exist.

No machine guns were required.

A relatively small number of people with boats, harpoons and an apparently inexhaustible food supply were enough.

The Great auk is a particularly nasty example of capitalism + collecting

Initially, people killed them because they were useful:

meat + eggs + fat + feathers.

Then they became rare.

And rarity made them more valuable.

Museums and wealthy collectors began paying substantial amounts for specimens and eggs. That created a perverse economic feedback loop:

fewer birds → rarer specimens → higher prices → greater incentive to kill the remaining birds.

The final pair were killed in 1844, and their single egg was crushed. Natural History Museum+1

So you can actually identify several layers of responsibility:

hunters → commercial demand → collectors/museums → market price.

There wasn't a single evil corporation responsible. It was a functioning market whose participants had almost no concept of the possibility that the commodity itself could disappear.

The passenger pigeon is the industrial-age version

This one is perhaps even more disturbing.

The passenger pigeon was once extraordinarily abundant. Hunters developed commercial methods for killing enormous numbers and selling the meat cheaply.

Telegraph and railway networks even made it possible for hunters to learn where enormous flocks had appeared and travel to them rapidly.

At the same time, forests were being cleared for agriculture and settlement.

So the causal chain became:

industrial agriculture + habitat destruction + commercial hunting + improved transport/communications

→ population collapse

→ hunting becomes even more efficient relative to the shrinking population

→ extinction.

The last known individual, Martha, died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Smithsonian Magazine

And this is where your "corporation vs country vs individuals" distinction gets interesting

There are roughly four types of human-caused extinction:

1. Small-group extinction

Steller's sea cow

A relatively small number of people can literally kill an entire species.

2. State/institution-enabled extinction

Thylacine

Government policy—in this case, bounty systems—can turn widespread persecution into an organised extermination programme. Tasmania Parks

3. Market-driven extinction

Great auk, passenger pigeon, rhinos

There doesn't need to be a single villain. Thousands of individually rational economic decisions can collectively produce an insane outcome.

4. Systemic civilisation-scale extinction

Baiji, Bramble Cay melomys

No individual necessarily intended the species' extinction. Instead, an enormous system—industrial development, pollution, climate change, fishing, shipping, etc.—creates cumulative pressure.

That last category is probably the most important for the present day.

The uncomfortable lesson from extinction history is that you don't actually need evil people to destroy a species.

You only need:

lots of people pursuing individually reasonable objectives + an ecological system whose limits aren't incorporated into the price of those objectives.

That is considerably more frightening than the story of a single villain.


You said:

You cannot evolve out of a clade. But some cunts get offended when we say we are monkeys. I mean in sense of monophyletic groups. So we all are simians, aren't we ?

ChatGPT said:

Yes. In the cladistic sense, humans are simians—and therefore monkeys.

The terminology causes unnecessary confusion because "monkey" has two different uses.

The taxonomy

Very roughly:

Primates
→ Haplorhini
→ Simiiformes (Anthropoidea)
→ Catarrhini
→ Hominoidea → humans, apes, gibbons
→ Hominidae → great apes
→ Homo → humans

The key point is that Simiiformes (the simians) is a clade. Humans are nested inside it.

5

And if you insist on monophyletic groups, you run into an amusing problem.

If by "monkeys" you mean:

all descendants of the common ancestor of monkeys

then apes are inside that evolutionary lineage too.

Humans didn't evolve from modern monkeys. Rather:

humans and modern monkeys share an ancient common ancestor.

But saying "humans aren't monkeys because humans evolved from monkeys" is therefore based on a misunderstanding. Evolution doesn't work as a ladder:

monkey → ape → human

It works more like a branching tree:






























                 ┌── modern monkey lineage
                 │
ancient simian ──┤
                 │       ┌── other apes
                 └───────┤
                         └── humans

So we didn't stop being simians when our lineage diverged from other simians.

And there's an even more delicious taxonomic consequence:

Humans are apes.

That's considerably less controversial scientifically.

We're hominids, hominoids, catarrhines, simians, primates, mammals, vertebrates, chordates, animals, and eukaryotes simultaneously.

Each category contains the ones below it.

So:

"Humans are apes."

True.

"Humans are simians."

True.

"Humans are primates."

True.

"Humans are mammals."

True.

"Humans are animals."

Also true.

The interesting bit is that "monkey" isn't a clean formal taxonomic group in the same way that Simiiformes is. In modern biological usage, monkey is largely a common-name grouping covering New World and Old World monkeys, while excluding apes in conventional usage.

So if you want to be maximally precise, I'd say:

Humans are simians, specifically catarrhine hominoids (apes).

If someone objects to "we are monkeys", they're often objecting to the everyday meaning of monkey, not the underlying evolutionary relationship.

And yes: you cannot evolve out of your ancestry. You can only become a different branch within it.
